A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same attack, and their text, figures and appendices support comparison. v1's appendix experiments can be matched to v3 Sections 4.7–4.8; v3's template catalogue is also readable.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-reconstruction experiments across diffusion models and controlled synthetic fine-tuning experiments in Appendix A.

after.justification: v3 retains original reconstruction and synthetic results and adds quantitative discovery analysis, a user study and experiments using recorded user prompts.

M1.justification: The attack retains collocation collection, pattern-prefixed prompts, segmentation and masking, CLIP similarity above 0.95, clique size of at least two, and manual source tracing. New template-group explanations and evaluations do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation using prompts from Midjourney's prompt dataset and DiffusionDB, plus human assessment of copying. These introduce naturally occurring inputs and an observer population. Existing model targets and synthetic Coffee Mug, Tea Cup and T-Shirt scenarios remain.

E2.justification: Webster remains the explicit one-step and ten-step comparator in v1 Figure 7 and v3 Figure 8. Reference examples and collocation sources from Somepalli and Hintersdorf remain. Added discussion of earlier works' computational budgets does not constitute a newly evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: New protocols include a study with 70 participants, 56 source images, 18–19 questions per participant, different-seed controls and A/B/Both/None responses. Section 4.5 also selects 35 short recorded prompts for regeneration: 20 from Midjourney and 15 from DiffusionDB. These are added evaluation designs, rather than established reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds template-discovery yield versus collocations tested in Figure 4 and human validation covering direct copying, interpolation and perturbations in Section 4.4. The synthetic leakage experiments and SD 3.5 memorization traces already existed in v1 Appendices A–B and are relocated.

E5.justification: v1 specifies generation seeds but reports no empirical confidence intervals. v3 introduces a mean and 95% confidence interval over five permutations in Figure 4 and cross-participant confidence intervals in Figure 11. These establish new uncertainty-reporting practices, without establishing additional repeated model-training runs.

E6.justification: v3 newly reports 63 templates from 112 tested collocations, a discovery-curve slope of 0.52, and participant-response distributions. Recorded-prompt experiments produce template-memorized images for 8/20 Midjourney prompts and 7/15 DiffusionDB prompts. Appendix A adds numerous template examples, and Figure 6 replaces the earlier dress example. These are added or revised findings, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. v3's discussion of many-to-many template groups is conceptual explanation, without a new mathematical definition or derivation; the existing similarity criterion remains unchanged.

C1.justification: The central claim of low-resource reconstruction through benign prompts without training-set access remains. The abstract and introduction add the specific claim that prompts actually recorded from users can reproduce memorized elements, extending the demonstration beyond researcher-constructed prompts.

C2.justification: The main interpolation, perturbation and leakage interpretations remain. v3 adds explanations of semantic and product-description links within template groups, a rationale for human assessment, and explicit limits on estimating real-world prevalence. It removes v1's explicit public-image and benign-edit scope statement and its broader deduplication recommendation.

D1.justification: v3 adds a collocation/template catalogue, instructions locating a collocation text file in the existing repository, prompt-dataset references and a total generation count of 11,400. However, its relocated synthetic experiment omits v1's 18 CC0 patterns, 54 image-caption pairs, LoRA specification and caption-construction details. This substantially changes reproducibility information without establishing a different underlying experiment.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for the Midjourney prompt dataset and DiffusionDB and removes the LoRA paper and Freepik reference entry. It further contrasts template-group associations with one-to-one extraction targeting while retaining the broader related-work coverage.

P1.justification: The introduction and phenomenon explanations undergo substantial rewriting. v1's Discussion and Limitations block disappears, appendix experiments move into expanded Results subsections, and a new catalogue appendix appears. v3 also contains overlapping comparison subsections, repeated explanations and unresolved cross-references.

P2.justification: v3 adds the recorded-prompt illustration, two statistical plots and an extensive illustrated catalogue, while resizing and rearranging existing montages. Former Figure 8 is displayed twice as Figures 7 and 12. Figure 6 changes an example and prompt labels, and its source/generated caption is inconsistent with retained image ordering.

improvement.justification: The recorded-prompt pilot and human study strengthen v1's largely qualitative evidence for unintentional copying, while the catalogue makes identified templates easier to inspect. The gain is limited: the selected prompt sample cannot establish real-world prevalence, synthetic reproducibility details are lost, and duplicated comparisons, unresolved references and inconsistent Figure 6 labels weaken reporting. The evidence supports a positive but limited overall improvement.
